beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Your inbox piles up, your calendar fills itself, and Claude can see none of it. The naive fix is to hand it your password. But the better question is the one on screen.

backspaces 'give Claude my passwords' -> 'connect Claude to my tools safely'

props.text: How do I give Claude my passwords

beats.narration_text: Three terms. A connector: the plug between Claude and one of your apps. Permissions: what you let it do — read, write, or send. An automation: a repeat job you hand it, like a morning email summary.

beats.narration_text: Right now, Claude lives in a chat window, and your real life lives somewhere else — your inbox, your calendar. So you copy things over by hand: paste the email, paste the invite. Connectors end the copying. The chat reaches into your apps, and talks about what's actually in them.

beats.narration_text: Here's how it works. You open your connectors settings, pick the app, and click connect. Then the app itself asks you to sign in — Google, Microsoft, whoever runs it. You never type your password into Claude. It's the same dance as logging into a new phone app with your Google account.

shot.visual_intent: The plug on its cable slides into the socket on the email app card; a shield with an ink check pops on the card (signed in). Label 'the plug' beside the card.

beats.narration_text: Then comes the screen that matters most: permissions. It lists exactly what Claude may do — read your email, read your calendar, send email. Reading is looking; sending is acting. So grant the smallest key that works. Start read-only. You can always widen it later.

beats.narration_text: Now the payoff. The first automation worth setting up: the morning brief. Every morning, you ask: what's my day, and what needs a reply? Claude reads your calendar and your unread email, and hands the day back in three lines — what's on, what needs you, what can wait.

beats.narration_text: The second: inbox triage. Point it at the pile and ask: what actually needs me? It sorts the real from the noise — the bill and the boss in one stack, newsletters and receipts in the other. You read what matters, and skip the rest.

beats.narration_text: The third is the companion to our meetings film. Before a call, ask: what do I need to know? It pulls the invite and the last thread with these people, and hands you a one-paragraph brief. You walk in already knowing the room.

beats.narration_text: Now what to watch out for. The big one is sending. A draft is Claude guessing; a sent email is you acting. So let it write every draft it wants — but nothing leaves your outbox until your own eyes have read it. The send button stays yours.

beats.narration_text: The second warning: give it the smallest key, and take keys back. If a job only needs reading, never grant sending. And every few months, open your connectors and pull the plugs you don't use anymore. An unused connection is an unlocked door.

shot.visual_intent: The app card with the plug in its socket; the plug slides out along its cable and lands in a tray; a check stamps the tray. Label 'pull the plug'.

beats.narration_text: And one more, because nobody tells you this. Once it's connected, Claude reads everything in the app — including a calendar invite from a total stranger. And a stranger can hide instructions in an invite that try to steer the AI. So: a weird invite from someone you don't know? Don't accept it. Don't ask Claude about it. Delete it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Connect one app — your email — and keep it read-only. Then paste this into Claude: Look at my unread emails from this week and give me a three-line summary. Read only — do not send, reply, or change anything. Then check two things yourself. One: did anything leave your inbox? Open your sent folder — it should be empty. Two: open your connectors settings — does the email connection show read access only? If it shows send, disconnect it and reconnect with fewer permissions.
